searchText: <@456226577798135808> In the stateless ethereum call you mentioned two strategies for migrating towards a merkelized code setting. From my reading/hearing, the first strategy is that * There exists an intermediate stage where the merkelizaion of code has not happened fully. Meaning some nodes chunk the code and some nodes don’t. Even the nodes that chunk the code need to maintain the code Hash, in addition to the Merkle Patricia trie. * So, all nodes maintain a map: chunk —> sets of jump destinations, it contains * Validation. If a miner who has done chunking sends the needed chunks for a transaction executing a contract call, then the miner with the whole code looks up the jumpdest table and collects the other chunks from its database, and stitches all the chunks, computes the hash of the whole code, and then checks with the stored code hash to ascertain that the sender has sent the chunks without tampering. * A stateless client cannot validate here. Only the validator with full code can validate. The next stage is where all nodes have merkelized code and are maintaining the Merkle Patricia trie. Then transition to the merkelized world, by replacing codeHashes with codeRoots through a hard fork. Am I right? I do not understand your second strategy, where you first determine the contracts that contain invalid jumps. Please elaborate. I meant slightly different two strategies. Number 1) perform the calculation of valid jump-dest at deployment (or one-off transformation), and prepend the list of valid jump dest to the code before computing merkle tree hash on it. So 1 or more first chunks will contain the list of valid jumpdest, and will always be part of the witness if the contract is invoked. Number 2) during deployment or one-off transformation, perform more sophisticated analysis, with the attempt to prove that regardless of the input and the state, the contract execution will never make an invalid jump. If the proving is successful, this is marked accordingly in the contract's object. Now, for contracts that are marked this way, code chunking can be done in any way, because it is known that invalid jumps never occur. For contracts that are not marked this way (it was not possible to prove the absense of invalid jumps), witness includes the entire bytecode Our hypothesis is that it is not too hard to make an algorithm where this analysis succeeds on overwhelming majority of contracts. For those where adversary introduces invalid jumps on purpose, or makes it unprovable, we use default strategy, which will make such contract more expensive to use Uninformed outsider here: is the code merklization scheme part of the consensus protocol or would it be up to clients to decide how to merklize it efficiently? it has to be part of the consensus do you assume a jumpdest approach of code-merkelization for the first approach? nope, I think we should just use fixed-sized chunks What is the role of the list of jumpdests? How does it help a stateless client to validate the sent chunks? it will help decide for any jump whether it is valid or not, which the main reason why we cannot simply chunk fixed size without some extra things because even if it looks like a jump going into a JUMPDEST opcode, it is not clear for a stateless client whether this JUMPDEST opcode is really opcode, or part of PUSHDATA <@259648573401071617> idea was to maintain a one byte along with the chunk that says the offset for the first instruction in the chunk I was thinking of the migration question that <@273808422753796097> asked. How do we go replacing the codehash with the trie structure globally and updating the state Merkle root? I thought you had two strategies that were not an one-shot approach. given that the size of the bytecode is still relatively small, I think it would be quite easy to do straightforward migration where everyone just re-hashes the contracts Would that require mainnet downtime? no Hardfork? hardfork would be required, because the way we calculate state root changes, but not for the migration migration to the binary tree would also be relatively easy in the world where all implementations use flat state data model. Yes, I understand that. So the two strategies that you described above are not for migration, I think you were describing code Merkelization approaches actually. Right? Yes, on the call I misunderstood the question Thanks for the clarification So, from the call we don't have any ideas for migration other than one shot. Right? correct. At this point, it seems like more complex strategies would be an overkill but there are lots of details even with the one-shot Like what? Please.. like (not exhaustive list) 1) will the cost of code-reading opcodes change and if yes, how? 2) what will EXTCODEHASH return? Could you version code so that you wouldn't have to rehash the state roots? If I'm understanding right, perhaps when a later merklized scheme is decided you could just change the version number

excerpts.author: 80raghavendra
excerpts.content:
<@456226577798135808> In the stateless ethereum call you mentioned two strategies for migrating towards a merkelized code setting. From my reading/hearing, the first strategy is that 
* There exists an intermediate stage where the merkelizaion of code has not happened fully. Meaning some nodes chunk the code and some nodes don’t. Even the nodes that chunk the code need to maintain the code Hash, in addition to the Merkle Patricia trie.
* So, all nodes maintain a map: chunk —> sets of jump destinations, it contains
* Validation. If a miner who has done chunking sends the needed chunks for a transaction executing a contract call, then the miner with the whole code looks up the jumpdest table and collects the other chunks from its database, and stitches all the chunks, computes the hash of the whole code, and then checks with the stored code hash to ascertain that the sender has sent the chunks without tampering.
* A stateless client cannot validate here. Only the validator with full code can validate.
The next stage is where all nodes have merkelized code and are maintaining the Merkle Patricia trie. Then transition to the merkelized world, by replacing codeHashes with codeRoots through a hard fork. Am I right?

I do not understand your second strategy, where you first determine the contracts that contain invalid jumps. Please elaborate.

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: I meant slightly different two strategies. Number 1) perform the calculation of valid jump-dest at deployment (or one-off transformation), and prepend the list of valid jump dest to the code before computing merkle tree hash on it. So 1 or more first chunks will contain the list of valid jumpdest, and will always be part of the witness if the contract is invoked.

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: Number 2) during deployment or one-off transformation, perform more sophisticated analysis, with the attempt to prove that regardless of the input and the state, the contract execution will never make an invalid jump. If the proving is successful, this is marked accordingly in the contract's object. Now, for contracts that are marked this way, code chunking can be done in any way, because it is known that invalid jumps never occur. For contracts that are not marked this way (it was not possible to prove the absense of invalid jumps), witness includes the entire bytecode

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: Our hypothesis is that it is not too hard to make an algorithm where this analysis succeeds on overwhelming majority of contracts. For those where adversary introduces invalid jumps on purpose, or makes it unprovable, we use default strategy, which will make such contract more expensive to use
